Here's the bad news first: This game is maybe 3-4 hours long. The puzzles aren't too terribly hard to figure out and there doesn't seem to be any branching paths to the narrative. Also, the blur effect on the cutscenes could be irritating to some.

The good news: It's a well-told story that IS short, but it's surprisingly punchy. A few of the puzzles are gripping to solve and the story builds consistently with intrigue and suspense as you go. It's all organic and nothing feels out of place. The soundtrack is *superbly* done with music fitting pretty much everything you're doing. 

$14 for 3 hours is kind of a steep ask for a video game, but considering how much it is to go to a movie theater these days and spend more for *less*, your mileage may vary. Worth it on a sale, I'd wager.

I want them to really sink in a longer story, more intrigue, more stuff to do, and give us the chance to find a better path than just one single narrative. 

Choice matters to the player and if we feel like nothing we did really changed anything on the main scenario, it can be jarring when the ending piledrives us with how things turned out despite our efforts. Food for thought, Bureau 81!

Anyways, I'm giving this a recommend. Your choice to wait for sale or not, but it's not so steep you won't enjoy yourself with a well-crafted and thought-out experience. Light on gaming, heavy on story and immersion.

It occasionaly introduces some interesting mechanisms (i was looking forward to trying the [spoiler]chemscan[/spoiler] again after learning how to use it), but then fails to include them throughout the story. Overall, it doesn't really let you "deduce" much past the first few days.

The ending is pretty abrubt and unsatisfying, as it leaves a lot of plotpoints unresolved and comes off as a bad cliffhanger for a second opus.

Overall, the game seems to be more preoccupied with its storytelling (which was not bad!) than with its gameplay (not great). Could've been a pretty good short film, but I don't recommend it as a game. It doesn't seem to trust their player or itself enough to rely on more complex game mechanics than simply "clicking the button when asked".

This game has everything I love. The operator is enjoyable from start to finish, and the story is an absolute banger. I was surprised to find voice acting, which I wasn’t expecting, but it added a lot to the experience. The characters are engaging, and I genuinely enjoyed speaking with them. The choices you can make during calls felt natural—definitely things I would have actually said, which was great.

The gameplay itself is pretty self-explanatory while still having some depth. Even though it’s mostly clicking and a bit of typing, it still managed to pull me in with the story. I felt a real sense of accomplishment whenever I solved something. At first, the story was incredibly gripping—I had no idea what was going on and was eager to piece it together. However, as it progressed towards the final parts, it became much easier to predict, and I had already figured things out before the game revealed them.

I was able to complete every achievement in a single playthrough, which took about 3-4 hours. If you enjoy mystery and crime investigation, you’ll probably love this.

Overall, I’d definitely recommend it to anyone, but maybe wait for a sale, as it could be considered pricey given its short length and relatively simple gameplay.

To the question of whether I'd recommend this game: it depends, but probably not. 

Full disclosure up-front: I knew nothing about this game, nor had I done any investigating as to what the game was ultimately meant to be, so my reactions here are likely influenced by it not being quite what I expected or really wanted. 

The Operator is a ultimately a fairly short, story-based narrative dressed in the clothing of a detective game, rather than a detective game where you work through puzzles and solve mysteries. 

The game's mechanics and design were an interesting approach to storytelling, but felt quite underused, which probably goes more to my expectations of wanting a detective puzzle game with a greater variety in cases to solve. In most instances a new mechanic was introduced for one section, only for it to never be used again. 

The story itself is passable. I've consumed my fair share of content in the thriller, detective, mystery and conspiracy genres, and nothing here felt fresh to me in terms of the plot; you could see where the story was going from a mile away and the ultimate outcomes fairly early on. 

If you want a mystery story with conspiracy elements woven in, then this is probably worth a go. If that's not what you're in the market for, then you can probably give this a miss.

So here's a recent and what I consider accurate short review.

The game is worth playing and given it's a bit over the length of a regular movie maybe 2 I'd say at the price of 15 - 25 it's reasonable given movie ticket and popcorn. Replay value isn't really there unless you forget what happened and replay a few years later, but who knows!

It's not really an investigation game and while I'm fine with linear games it is important to mention the plot largely is linear and the actions you can take are too. It's generous with the help in most cases too. It's more like an interactable movie from the main interface of a computer.

The plot and such isn't anything too crazy if you've seen Bourne and Mission Impossible and stuff like that, but it's a pretty good one.

The bomb segment is probably the best part, but it is an absolutely shame that the defusal process is NOT random but instead always the same thing. They had so much information for alternative bombs after all. The ending is highly depressing and ultimately doesn't make a lot of sense due to the wiping the servers and such. I think it should have kept that held back for a potential sequel.

I'd of liked more investigation options, more possibilities to really need to assess things. But I would be interested in a sequel or another game expanding on the systems.

Is it worth a purchase? Yes. And it does really good job at being voluminous in the details and subject matter that they're going into, sometimes a bit too confusingly haha. Whether that's technobabble or someone knew what they were writing about is hard to say. And the voice acting is solid too.

Makes no sense the agents don't have a partner with them at all times tho.

--- I recommend this purchase as a story focused gamer.
Other games you might want to consider that I've played recently that are also story focused or just good: Escape Simulator, Hades, Operation Tango, 	The Operator (this one), Roottree (tho it's less like a game), StarCraft 2 especially Legacy, We Were Here series sequels (but it can be hard at times), Ixion, Strange Horticulture, and a few others.

Thanks for reading --- February 2025.

Edit: As a side note, while the developer seems very pleased with its soundtrack there were a lot of times I didn't really hear any music going on which seemed a bit odd, like during the first server room pursuit to reveal some data.

The game has a great concept and some thrilling moments. The developers did a fantastic job immersing you in the feeling of being a "cog in a machine". The music, interface design, story theme, and execution were excellent. I especially enjoyed the quiet moments where I could read through various documents and explore the backstory and world the developers created.

That’s why it pains me so much that all this hard work feels utterly underutilized. You’re essentially handheld and dragged through a linear story, with little to no impact from your choices. There are intricate mechanics that seem fun once you struggle through their first use, but they are never used again. It is just a little bit more "game" than a "interactive movie".

I don’t want to be cruel—I can see the developers put a lot of effort into it—but it was just far too short.
